reasons: A1: Reported effort release is measured, but no matched quality baseline, defect outcome, accuracy result or retained-quality comparison substantiates quality improvement.
A2: Governed prompts, deterministic rescoring and the documented QLoRA design show thoughtful adaptation, but deployed-model identity and comparative uplift are unproved.
A3: Two reported quarters, training, reusable prompts and configurable controls indicate adaptability; usage records, model runs and longitudinal evaluation remain absent.
A4: The 257 person-days and eight-to-four-hour example are carefully scoped and net of reported review, but the ledger, calculation and approvals are not attached.
A5: The paper identifies operational users and preserves specialist review, but supplies no stakeholder satisfaction, service-user benefit or verified assurance outcome.
editorial_fixes: Replace "The IntelliA11y AI SDLC workspace was observed with seven configurable AI controls" with "A local IntelliA11y development workspace was observed with seven configurable AI controls" to prevent the observation being read as client deployment evidence.

In the summary, replace "The account team reports 257 person-days of released effort" with "The account narrative reports 257 person-days of released effort" so the attribution matches S01 and does not imply inspection of the reporting team or system.
Keep the 85% activity-coverage sentence only once, as drafted, and do not elevate it into the outcomes section until its population and period are defined.
missing_evidence: Underlying Pulse task ledger, review deductions, calculation method and approval provenance for the 257 person-days.
Matched pre/post quality evidence for AI-assisted test artefacts, including sampling method, defects, completeness and reviewer acceptance.
Defined numerator, denominator, period and source for the reported 85% accessibility activity coverage.
Deployed-model identity, representative run records and an independently curated holdout with baseline-versus-adapted-model results.
Stakeholder satisfaction or verified downstream assurance and service-user outcomes.

reasons: N1: N01 shows achieved workload volume and correct failure detection against explicit P90 thresholds, but only four displayed samples per transaction and no closure result limit substantiation.

N2: Production-traffic analysis, six profiles, Kubernetes scaling checks and abnormal cache-pattern reproduction give a strong representative-condition case, though primary run artefacts remain limited.
N3: The method exposes release risks and the narrative links testing to three releases and migration decisions; sign-offs, dates, reruns and observation windows are absent.
N4: Goals, roles, tools and reusable assets are specific, but the principal efficiency, capacity and release achievements remain narrative claims rather than primary records.
N5: Daily rebuilds, invalid success exits, cache reproduction and missing telemetry are concrete challenges with credible engineering responses; quantitative remediation closure is incomplete.
editorial_fixes: Remove the paragraph beginning "AI supported the engineering of these capabilities" because its incremental contribution is unquantified and it distracts from the non-functional evidence without helping a criterion.
Replace "The framework has been applied to AKS migration programmes" with "The delivery narrative reports application of the framework to AKS migration work" to preserve source attribution.

In the summary, replace "A custom JMeter simulation reproduced abnormal cache growth for remediation testing" with "The supplied case narrative reports that a custom JMeter simulation reproduced abnormal cache growth for remediation testing" because N02 is a narrative digest, not raw output.
missing_evidence: Raw representative workload runs showing transaction mix, sample counts, environment comparability, acceptance criteria and sufficient percentile populations.
Matched cache baseline and retest with workload equivalence, duration, cache or memory measurements, change identifier and reviewer acceptance.
Before/after task timings, run count, measurement period, review effort and exception handling for each reported greater-than-90% reduction.
Release dates, readiness sign-offs, defect closure and defined post-release observation windows for the three reported releases and migration decision.
Gate rerun showing restored telemetry coverage and reconciled endpoint-level versus aggregate performance results.

reasons: I1: Distributed domain ownership with centrally governed shared execution is a credible practice advance, but active contribution and comparative benefit are not evidenced.
I2: The bottleneck, ownership model, tag convention, generator and three-pipeline implementation are clearly described; code and run history were not inspected.
I3: The model attempts a transferable multi-team contribution pattern, but evidence of boundary-pushing effect, comparative novelty or broader influence is presently too thin for 4/5.
I4: Goals and responsibilities are coherent, while five-team adoption and delivered assets remain source assertions with no contribution, execution or outcome records.
I5: The paper evaluates maintenance, inconsistent setup, triage and execution-environment constraints with plausible responses; an end-to-end failure-to-owner-to-rerun example is absent.
editorial_fixes: Replace "The source describes five service teams using the onboarding approach" with "The source reports five service teams onboarded to the approach" to keep adoption attribution consistent and avoid implying verified active use.
Replace "The delivered assets described in the source are" with "The source describes the delivered assets as" because the repositories and pipeline implementation have not been inspected.
Retain the current exclusion of separate AI savings and demonstrations; do not reintroduce them as Innovation results.
missing_evidence: Contribution history, tagged-test inventory and shared-suite run records for each of the five reported teams.
Repository evidence for the template utility and three pipelines, including successful and failed executions.
A complete triage example from contributed-test failure through ownership assignment, correction and successful rerun.
Matched setup timings with identical scope and validation effort.
Measured reduction in duplicate maintenance, change in regression coverage, cross-service defects found or comparison with the prior operating model.

council_recommendation: The revised papers are materially more accurate and submission-ready as narratives, but none meets the target of 4/5 on every criterion. NFT is strongest at 17/25 because it has direct workload and failure-detection observations plus specific challenge responses. AI remains 11/25 because efficiency is not accompanied by measured quality or stakeholder outcomes. Innovation remains 13/25 because implementation, adoption and comparative effect are still narrative assertions. Apply only the attribution and scope edits listed above; further scoring gains require primary records or new measurements, not additional prose. Keep the three populations separate and preserve the evidence-pack warnings that hashes and source digests establish traceability rather than truth.
